questions.title: BX and BP are different registers
questions.question: Which pair names the same register family at different widths?
questions.explanation: EBP is the low 32-bit view of RBP. BX/EBX/RBX and BP/EBP/RBP are distinct families. P means pointer in BP/SP; X is part of the historical AX/BX/CX/DX names.

questions.title: Names do not force every use
questions.question: Must RDI always contain a destination pointer because DI historically means destination index?
options: Yes. It cannot contain an integer.
Yes. RDI automatically dereferences its value.
No. RDI is another name for RDX.
No. Instructions and the calling convention determine its current role.
questions.explanation: A historical name does not attach a C type to the bits. Some instructions have fixed roles; ordinary MOV and arithmetic can use RDI as data.

questions.title: An address differs from its contents
questions.question: RDI=4096 and the eight-byte value at address 4096 is 23. What does movq (%rdi),%rax produce?
questions.explanation: MOV uses RDI to locate the source memory. It reads the value there without changing the pointer. In C this is like reading *p, rather than copying p.

questions.title: Copy, dereference or calculate
questions.question: RBX=4096; the eight-byte value at 4096 is 23. Which sequence of RAX results matches movq %rbx,%rax; movq (%rbx),%rax; leaq (%rbx),%rax, considered separately?
questions.explanation: MOV with a register source copies the address value. MOV with a memory source loads its contents. LEA calculates the address expression and does not load memory.

questions.title: A wide pointer can load a small object
questions.question: In movl (%rdi),%eax, how many bytes of data are loaded, and what supplies the address?
options: Four bytes; the 64-bit value in RDI supplies the address
Four bytes from the address in EAX
Only one byte because parentheses select a byte
questions.explanation: The l suffix and EAX choose four-byte data. RDI supplies a separate 64-bit address. Address width does not dictate object width.

questions.title: A 32-bit address form can be valid
questions.question: In x86-64 mode, which statement about movl (%ebx),%eax is correct?
options: It always fails to assemble in 64-bit mode
It reads eight bytes because addresses are 64-bit
It is equivalent to using the full RBX value for every possible RBX
It can encode a 32-bit address calculation, zero-extended into the low 4 GiB
questions.explanation: The address-size override allows a 32-bit effective address. This does not make EBX an ordinary full-width C pointer. The address must still map accessible memory. AX is not a valid address base.

questions.title: Recall the argument order
questions.question: For the Linux x86-64 convention here, which order matches the first six integer or pointer arguments?
options: RCX, RDX, R8, R9, RDI, RSI
RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI
RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9
RDI, RDX, RSI, RCX, R8, R9
questions.explanation: Dogs Steal Donuts; Cats Ate Nine recalls D,S,D,C,8,9. It is a mnemonic for this convention. Windows x64 instead starts RCX,RDX,R8,R9. The convention is separate from the historical register names.

questions.title: Separate RBX, RBP and RSP
questions.question: A function uses a conventional frame pointer. Which register normally provides that stable frame reference?
options: RIP because it points at local variables
questions.explanation: RBP can remain stable while RSP changes. RSP tracks the stack top; RBX is a separate general-purpose, callee-saved register. A frame pointer is optional.

questions.title: Carry and signed overflow are different
questions.question: An eight-bit ADD computes 127+1, leaving 0x80. Which flags describe that result?
questions.explanation: The stored pattern is signed -128, so SF=1. Positive signed inputs produced a negative result, so OF=1. Unsigned 128 fits in eight bits, so CF=0; the result is nonzero.

questions.title: CMP uses subtraction borrow
questions.question: For eight-bit unsigned values, CMP computes 3−5 without storing it. What are CF and ZF?
questions.explanation: Subtraction needs an unsigned borrow when destination < source, so CF=1. The operands differ, so ZF=0. Calling every CF event a carry out obscures subtraction.

questions.title: Compare with a constant
questions.question: After cmpq $3,%rdi, which jump selects the signed condition x<3?
options: jb small for every signed x
js small for every signed x
questions.explanation: CMP computes x−3. JL uses SF≠OF to implement signed less-than, including cases where that subtraction overflows.

questions.title: Select one of two constants
questions.cCode: long choose(long x) { if(x<3) return 1; return 2; }
questions.hint: Compare x with 3; branch to the return-1 path only when the signed comparison is less.
solutions:
cmpq $3,%rdi
jl small
movq $2,%rax
ret
small:
movq $1,%rax
ret
questions.explanation: Compare x with 3; branch to the return-1 path only when the signed comparison is less.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: Preserve subtraction order
questions.question: For signed x=2,y=7, an absolute-difference function takes the x<=y path. Which expression belongs there?
questions.explanation: The smaller value must be subtracted from the larger. Equality produces zero on either subtraction path.

questions.title: Translate both subtraction paths
questions.cCode:
// Precondition: the nonnegative difference fits in long.
long absdiff(long x,long y) { if(x>y) return x-y; return y-x; }
questions.hint: CMP sets the ordering without replacing x or y. JLE sends x<=y to y−x; otherwise compute x−y.
solutions:
cmpq %rsi,%rdi
jle other
movq %rdi,%rax
subq %rsi,%rax
ret
other:
movq %rsi,%rax
subq %rdi,%rax
ret
questions.explanation: CMP sets the ordering without replacing x or y. JLE sends x<=y to y−x; otherwise compute x−y.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: Reuse a result’s zero flag
questions.question: After addq $5,%rax, which jump directly checks whether the stored result is zero?
questions.explanation: ADD sets ZF from its stored result, so JE can use that fact without another CMP. LEA would not set ZF.

questions.title: Do not reinterpret arbitrary flags as CMP result,0
questions.question: An eight-bit ADD has result 0x80, SF=1, OF=1, ZF=0. Which statements are true?
options: JS and JG would both be taken with these flags
questions.explanation: JS reads SF. JG reads !ZF and SF==OF, which are also true here. JG after an arbitrary overflowing ADD is not simply a sign test of the stored result. Use TEST result,result to establish result-versus-zero flags first.

questions.title: Widen with zeros
questions.question: AL=0x80. What value does movzbl %al,%eax produce in RAX?
options: It preserves all old upper bits
questions.explanation: The byte is zero-extended to EAX=0x00000080. Writing EAX also clears RAX’s upper 32 bits. Widening preserves unsigned byte magnitude.

questions.title: Load an unsigned byte as a long
questions.cCode: unsigned long widen_byte(unsigned char x) { return x; }
questions.hint: Read the byte input in DIL and fill the wider destination with zeros.
questions.explanation: Read the byte input in DIL and fill the wider destination with zeros.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: Preserve a negative byte’s meaning
questions.question: AL=0x80. What does movsbq %al,%rax produce?
questions.explanation: The source sign bit is one, so all 56 added upper bits become one. The resulting 64-bit two’s-complement value is −128.

questions.title: Load a signed byte as a long
questions.cCode: long widen_signed(signed char x) { return x; }
questions.hint: Read the source at its declared byte width, then repeat its sign bit in the widened result.
questions.explanation: Read the source at its declared byte width, then repeat its sign bit in the widened result.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: An EAX write is not a signed long conversion
questions.question: EAX contains 0xffffffff, interpreted as signed int −1. Which instruction produces signed long −1 in RAX?
questions.explanation: MOVSLQ sign-extends 32 bits to 64. A 32-bit MOV instead zeroes the upper half, giving positive 4294967295 in RAX.

questions.title: Convert a signed int to long
questions.hint: MOVSLQ extends the sign of the 32-bit argument. MOVL alone is only appropriate for an unsigned widening.
questions.explanation: MOVSLQ extends the sign of the 32-bit argument. MOVL alone is only appropriate for an unsigned widening.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: SETcc writes one byte
questions.question: RAX=0x1122334455667788. A true condition executes sete %al. What is RAX?
questions.explanation: SETE writes 01 to AL. It preserves all seven other bytes, so the complete register is not automatically the integer 1.

questions.title: Store a condition instead of jumping
questions.question: What is the difference between je label and sete %al?
options: SETE changes ZF to match AL
JE may change the next instruction; SETE writes 0 or 1 and continues
JE writes the result into RAX
questions.explanation: Both inspect ZF. Neither clears flags. SETE stores a Boolean byte without branching.

questions.title: Finish a Boolean result
questions.question: After cmpq %rsi,%rdi; setg %al, what makes a complete 0-or-1 int in EAX without destroying that byte?
questions.explanation: Zero-extension retains AL’s 0 or 1 and defines the rest of EAX. Clearing EAX afterward would erase the result. Clearing before CMP is another valid strategy.

questions.title: Return a clean comparison result
questions.cCode:
// Also clear RAX above the int result.
int greater(long x,long y) { return x>y; }
questions.hint: CMP handles signed ordering. SETG produces a byte; MOVZBL normalizes the full return register.
questions.explanation: CMP handles signed ordering. SETG produces a byte; MOVZBL normalizes the full return register.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: Choose signed or unsigned SETcc
questions.question: After comparing x with y, which byte result implements unsigned x<y?
questions.explanation: SETB reads CF (unsigned borrow). SETL instead reads SF≠OF for signed less-than.

questions.title: Non-equality has its own mnemonic
questions.question: Which instruction writes a byte equal to one when ZF=0?
questions.explanation: SETNE is not-equal/nonzero; SETE tests ZF=1. The conditions correspond to JNE and JE respectively.

questions.title: A Boolean can be stored directly
questions.question: RDX points to a four-byte object whose bytes are aa bb cc dd. A true condition executes sete (%rdx). What are its bytes afterward?
questions.explanation: SETcc stores exactly one byte. Other bytes and the address register stay unchanged.

questions.title: Store one Boolean byte
questions.hint: Compare x with y, then SETE into the byte at the pointer in RDX.
questions.explanation: SETE writes a byte directly to memory. It does not overwrite adjacent bytes or the pointer.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; unsigned char is one byte

questions.title: A label is a code destination
questions.question: In if(x<=y) goto other;, what happens when x>y?
options: Execution falls through to the next statement
questions.explanation: A conditional transfer occurs only when the condition is true. Otherwise execution continues sequentially.

questions.title: A do-while executes before testing
questions.question: A loop body increments visits. Initially x=0. A do { visits++; } while(x); body runs how many times?
questions.explanation: The initial condition is tested only after the first body execution. Since x remains zero, the loop then stops.

questions.title: Count iterations of a do-while
questions.cCode: long bit_visits(unsigned long x) { long n=0; do { n++; x>>=1; } while(x); return n; }
questions.hint: The body runs once for x=0. SHR sets ZF from the updated x, so JNE repeats while it remains nonzero.
solutions:
movl $0,%eax
body:
incq %rax
shrq $1,%rdi
jne body
ret
questions.explanation: The body runs once for x=0. SHR sets ZF from the updated x, so JNE repeats while it remains nonzero.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: Keep the entry guard
questions.question: A bottom-tested loop body is used to implement while(x!=0). What preserves the initial-zero case?
options: A test and exit jump before the first body execution
questions.explanation: The entry guard skips the body when x starts zero. The bottom test controls subsequent repeats.

questions.title: Use a guarded bottom-test loop
questions.cCode: long while_visits(unsigned long x) { long n=0; while(x) { n++; x>>=1; } return n; }
questions.hint: Guard the first body execution with TEST/JE, then use SHR/JNE at the bottom.
solutions:
movl $0,%eax
testq %rdi,%rdi
je done
body:
incq %rax
shrq $1,%rdi
jne body
done:
ret
questions.explanation: Guard the first body execution with TEST/JE, then use SHR/JNE at the bottom.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: Account for all parts of for
questions.question: For for(i=0; i<n; i++), which order is correct?
options: Test once; repeat the body forever
Initialize once; test; body; update; return to test
Initialize on every iteration; body; test
questions.explanation: A for loop has initialization, a condition before each body, and an update after each completed body. The update is not the first action.

questions.title: Translate a for loop completely
questions.cCode:
// Precondition: 0<=n<=10000.
long triangular(long n) { long s=0; for(long i=0;i<n;i++) s+=i; return s; }
questions.hint: Initialize i and sum once; test i<n before the body; add i, then increment i before jumping back.
solutions:
movl $0,%eax
movl $0,%ecx
check:
cmpq %rdi,%rcx
jge done
addq %rcx,%rax
incq %rcx
jmp check
done:
ret
questions.explanation: Initialize i and sum once; test i<n before the body; add i, then increment i before jumping back.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: Count ones rather than positions
questions.question: For x=0b10110, successive low bits examined by x&1 before shifting are 0,1,1,0,1. What is the population count?
questions.explanation: Each one contributes one to the accumulator. Zero bits and leading positions do not add to the count.

questions.title: Combine a mask, shift and loop
questions.cCode: long count_ones(unsigned long x) { long result=0; do { result+=x&1UL; x>>=1; } while(x); return result; }
questions.hint: Save x’s low bit in RDX, add it to the result, then shift x. JNE must use SHR’s flags, not ADD’s.
solutions:
movl $0,%eax
body:
movq %rdi,%rdx
andl $1,%edx
addq %rdx,%rax
shrq $1,%rdi
jne body
ret
questions.explanation: Save x’s low bit in RDX, add it to the result, then shift x. JNE must use SHR’s flags, not ADD’s.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: A load need not visit RAM sticks
questions.question: Does movq (%rdi),%rax necessarily fetch data from the computer’s RAM chips on every execution?
options: Yes. A cache cannot hold ordinary program data.
No. The memory load may be satisfied by a CPU cache.
Yes. Parentheses force a trip to RAM.
No. It is always a register-to-register copy.
questions.explanation: The instruction accesses program memory. How the processor supplies those bytes is an implementation detail; caches often satisfy the access.

questions.title: Choose correct meaning before optimizing
questions.question: Which is the safest general statement about AX, EAX and RAX operations?
options: Choose the required width; performance depends on the instruction, dependencies and CPU.
AX is always slower than RAX
Every MOV takes exactly one cycle
RAX is only needed for positive values above four billion
questions.explanation: Widths define behavior. Some 32-bit forms are shorter and avoid upper-bit dependencies; partial-register effects and instruction encoding costs depend on the specific case. Sixty-four-bit types require their full semantics even when the current value is small.

questions.title: Basic asm is a compiler extension
questions.question: What does __asm__("nop"); inside a C function ask GCC to do?
options: Execute a C string at runtime
Run a separate assembler process at every function call
Automatically discover all changed C variables
Insert the given assembler text into the generated program
questions.explanation: GCC passes the template into its assembly output. It does not interpret the text as C or infer a complete input/output contract. __asm__ is accepted even in strict C modes as a GNU extension.

questions.title: Separate C strings from instructions
questions.question: Inside a template, what does "movq %1,%0;" "addq $1,%0" mean at the C string level?
options: A C addition of the strings
A guarantee that both instructions take one clock tick
Adjacent string literals concatenate; semicolons separate assembler instructions
questions.explanation:
C joins adjacent quoted strings. The assembler can separate instructions with semicolons; 
	 can instead format new instruction lines.

questions.title: Read the colon-separated contract
questions.question: What is the order in __asm__(template : ... : ... : ...)?
questions.explanation: The first section describes written C operands; the second describes read C expressions; the third names additional changed state. Empty sections still need colons when a later section is present.

questions.title: GCC places the operands
questions.question: Who chooses the actual register for an operand constrained with "r"?
options: GCC’s register allocator, subject to the declared constraints
questions.explanation: An r constraint permits a register; it does not name one. GCC emits needed input setup and makes the output available as the bound C variable.

questions.title: Placeholders differ from literal registers
questions.question: In extended asm, how do %0 and %%rax differ?
options: %%rax is needed in every standalone .s file
%0 substitutes operand zero; %%rax emits the literal register name %rax
questions.explanation: Extended templates use percent substitutions. A doubled percent emits one literal percent. Basic asm has no operand substitution and uses ordinary register percent spelling.

questions.title: Outputs come before inputs
questions.question: An asm has one output "=r"(out) and inputs "r"(x), "r"(y). What does %2 name?
questions.explanation: Output zero is numbered first. The two explicit inputs are numbered one and two. These numbers are operand positions, not register numbers.

questions.title: A fresh output does not need an old value
questions.question: The template overwrites result before reading it. Which output constraint is appropriate?
questions.explanation: = marks a write-only output. + declares that an initial value is read as well as written, which requires a meaningful initialized input.

questions.title: Repair an uninitialized read/write operand
questions.question: long result; followed by asm(... : "+r"(result) : ...), where the template only produces a new result, has which issue?
options: It incorrectly declares an initial input value; use a write-only output.
It forces result to be returned through RDI
It requires an extra pair of parentheses around result
questions.explanation: A read/write constraint claims the old C value is supplied. Do not use it for an uninitialized variable that should only receive a new value.

questions.title: A read/write value must start defined
questions.question: long result=x; is followed by a template multiplying result by y. Which constraint describes result?
questions.explanation: The old result is an input and the new result is an output. + describes both uses.

questions.title: Declare changed flags
questions.question: An inline template executes IMUL. Which extra state should its contract declare as changed?
options: No state, because C cannot name flags
questions.explanation: IMUL changes condition-code state. The cc clobber tells GCC not to carry assumptions about flags across the asm.

questions.title: Register and memory constraints name locations
questions.question: What does "+m"(*p) describe?
options: All program memory must be overwritten
The pointed-to memory object is both read and written
The pointer register p is incremented
The result must go in RAX
questions.explanation: m identifies a memory operand; + marks read/write data flow. *p describes the object, while p by itself is the address value.

questions.title: A pointer input is not a memory declaration
questions.question: Does "r"(p) alone tell GCC that the asm writes the object at p?
options: No. Declare the memory output or an appropriate memory clobber.
Yes, because p is a pointer
No, pointers cannot be asm inputs
questions.explanation: A register input supplies the pointer bits. It does not by itself declare a read or write through those bits.

questions.title: Declare fixed scratch registers
questions.question: A template uses literal RAX and RDX as temporary registers and IMUL changes flags. Which clobbers describe those changes?
options: No clobbers if the result is correct for 13 and 7
questions.explanation: Clobber names omit %. GCC avoids conflicts with those fixed scratch registers and accounts for their changed state. Outputs should be described as outputs, not duplicated as clobbers.

questions.title: A clobber is information, not a forced reload
questions.question: What does listing "rdx" in the clobbers guarantee?
options: RDX becomes a C output variable
GCC accounts for RDX being changed when allocating and preserving live values
GCC always reloads the same RDX value after the asm
questions.explanation: A clobber does not request a particular reload sequence. The compiler may save, move, recompute or avoid placing a live value there.

questions.title: Protect inputs that are read later
questions.question: A template first writes output %0, then later reads input %2. Why might "=&r" be needed for output %0?
options: It preserves the CPU flags automatically
It prevents that early output write from sharing a register with an input still needed
It initializes the result to zero
It makes the output a memory address
questions.explanation: Without &, GCC normally assumes inputs are consumed before outputs are produced. A multi-instruction template can violate that assumption.

questions.title: Find the register-overlap failure
questions.question: Template: movq %1,%0; addq %2,%0. What if GCC placed %0 and %2 in the same register?
options: The MOV would overwrite the second input before ADD reads it
The addition would always still be x+y
The assembler would necessarily reject the program
questions.explanation: The first instruction replaces the output register. If input two shares it, its original value is lost. Early-clobber forbids that overlap.

questions.title: Volatile does not replace operands
questions.question: Does asm volatile automatically declare all modified registers and memory?
options: Yes, all memory is automatically refreshed
Yes, it is a CPU serialization fence
No. Inputs, outputs and clobbers must still be accurate.
questions.explanation: Volatile restricts compiler removal and certain motion of the asm. It does not describe omitted data flow or automatically serialize the CPU.

questions.title: Compiler barrier versus hardware fence
questions.question: What does the "memory" clobber do?
options: Forces RDTSC to execute in order
Tells GCC about otherwise-unlisted memory effects and constrains compiler memory assumptions
questions.explanation: A memory clobber is a compiler-level memory barrier. It does not itself emit a processor fence or guarantee hardware instruction ordering.

questions.title: Inspect native code around the template
questions.question: What does objdump -d sample.o show?
options: Proof that all operand constraints are correct
Decoded machine instructions from the object’s executable sections
The runtime values of every input
questions.explanation: Disassembly shows both template instructions and surrounding compiler-generated setup/use. One build’s register choices do not prove the constraints work under every optimization.

questions.title: Follow inputs through a complete product
questions.question: For inline_product(13,7), with a correct initialized +r result and IMUL, what value should C receive?
questions.explanation: GCC provides the input operands; IMUL computes 13×7; the output binding makes that value available to the C return.

questions.title: Read the counter halves in the right order
questions.question: RDTSC writes the low 32 bits to which register, and the high 32 bits to which register?
questions.explanation: RDTSC returns the counter as EDX:EAX, with EDX the high half. It is the instruction name RDTSC, not RSTSC.

questions.title: A counter read is not a duration
questions.question: What does a single RDTSC reading provide?
options: The exact number of instructions executed
The current CPU frequency in hertz
A time-stamp counter value; an interval needs two readings
Seconds since the previous C function call
questions.explanation: The counter is not automatically relative to your previous invocation. On invariant-TSC systems its rate is not the current changing core clock frequency.

questions.title: Widen before shifting a 32-bit half
questions.question: Why is ((unsigned long)high<<32) used instead of high<<32 when high is a 32-bit unsigned int?
options: It reverses the high and low halves
The cast makes the left operand 64-bit before the shift
The cast forces a memory access
A shift by 32 is always valid for 32-bit operands
questions.explanation: C requires the shift count to be smaller than the promoted left operand’s width. Widen first so the count 32 is valid and the high half is retained.

questions.title: Combine supplied counter halves
questions.cCode: unsigned long join_counter(unsigned int low,unsigned int high) { return ((unsigned long)high<<32) | low; }
questions.hint: Zero-extend each 32-bit half. Shift the high half left 32 places, then OR in the low half. These are supplied values, not a live counter read.
questions.explanation: Zero-extend each 32-bit half. Shift the high half left 32 places, then OR in the low half. These are supplied values, not a live counter read.
questions.dataModel: Linux x86-64 LP64; int 32 bits, long and pointers 64 bits; AT&T source, destination

questions.title: Define what the first call means
questions.question: A ticks function starts last=0 and immediately returns current−last. What does its first result represent?
options: The number of instructions in main
The current counter value measured from zero, not an interval between two calls
questions.explanation: No previous invocation reading has been recorded yet. A separate initialized flag can make the first-call policy explicitly return zero.

questions.title: Keep state across invocations
questions.question: A saved previous counter is 900. The next reading is 950. What should the function return and save?
questions.explanation: Subtract the previous reading to get the interval, then update the saved reading for the next call. Static storage persists between calls.

questions.title: Use unsigned counter subtraction
questions.question: For 64-bit unsigned counters, previous=2^64−3 and current=2 after one wrap. What is current−previous modulo 2^64?
questions.explanation: The unsigned subtraction wraps modulo 2^64: three increments reach zero and two more reach two. This is meaningful only with the intended counter continuity and interval assumptions.

questions.title: Repair the assembler notation
questions.question: Which standalone AT&T instruction stores ECX to label + RDX + RBX*4?
questions.explanation: The opcode has no trailing comma. The memory displacement label is not an immediate, and the address scale is written as bare 4. These are assembler syntax rules; inline code still needs a correct compiler contract.

questions.title: Identify what actually repeats the body
questions.question: A population-count sequence ends its body with shrq $1,%rdi; jne body, then reaches a return sometimes printed as rep ret. What controls repetition of the body?
options: The REP prefix repeats the entire function
JNE tests the flags left by SHR
RET checks whether RDI is zero
RAX automatically jumps back whenever its value changes
questions.explanation: JNE repeats while the updated x is nonzero. The prefix sometimes shown with RET is not the loop condition or a repetition of the whole function. The lab uses plain RET.
